# Remote SDK config (Data Collection)

Remote SDK config decides, per group of browsers, what the browser SDK sends right away, what it keeps on the device in case it is needed, and what it drops, without shipping a new build.

- **Who has it**: browser projects (React, Vue.js, Svelte, jQuery) whose app runs the 2.x browser SDK (`@tracewayapp/frontend` 2.x or a wrapper of the same version; npm `latest`), Flutter projects whose app runs the Flutter SDK 2.x prerelease (`flutter pub add 'traceway:^2.0.0-beta.1'`), iOS projects whose app runs the iOS SDK 2.x prerelease (Swift Package Manager, `from: "2.0.0-beta.1"`), and Android projects whose app runs the Android SDK 2.x prerelease (`implementation("com.tracewayapp:traceway:2.0.0-beta.1")`). The 1.x SDKs and the React Native SDK never ask for settings. Backend projects and the other mobile projects have no Data Collection page, and the API refuses them with 403.
- **Where**: **Data Collection** in the sidebar (`/data-collection`), shown for browser, Flutter, iOS and Android projects. It lists the **Rules** in order (enable switch, move up and down, edit, delete) with **Preview** and **New Rule**, and below them the **Captures** with their status, refreshed every 15 seconds, and **New Capture**.
- **How it travels**: the SDK polls Traceway over OpAMP at start, every 5 minutes by default (`OPAMP_POLL_INTERVAL_SECONDS` on self-hosted servers), when a tab becomes visible after that interval, and when the app calls `refreshConfig()`. There is no push, so a saved change reaches a browser at its next poll.

## Modes and defaults

Every signal is in one mode: **stream** (sent within about a second), **buffer** (kept on the device, sent only when a trigger flushes it or a capture starts) or **off** (dropped, though triggers still see it).

| Signal | Covers | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `errors`, `messages` | Exceptions, `captureMessage` | stream |
| `network` | `fetch` and XHR, as CLIENT spans | buffer |
| `console`, `navigation`, `userActions`, `custom` | Console and `log()` lines (info and above), route changes, clicks, `track()` and `recordAction()` | buffer |
| `webVitals` | Detailed LCP, INP, CLS events | buffer |
| `resourceTiming` | Page and asset load timings | off |
| `longTasks` | Main-thread blocks of 50 ms or more (`browser.long_task`, Chromium only) | off |
| `routeTiming` | How long single-page-app route changes take to render (`browser.route_timing`) | off |
| replay | rrweb session replay | buffer |

**Flutter projects** use the same document. Their signals are `errors`, `messages`, `console` (`print` / `debugPrint`), `network` (dart:io HTTP client spans), `navigation`, `userActions` (taps, with a widget selector), `custom` (`Traceway.track`, `Traceway.recordAction`) and replay (an MP4 screen recording or a wireframe, buffered as the last `maxBufferFrames` frames, about 10 seconds at 15 fps, and streamed as segments during a capture); the rule editor hides the browser-only signals. `replay.captureMode` (**Replay type** in the rule editor) switches a Flutter app between `video` and `wireframe`, the widget tree replayed as HTML; unset keeps the app's `screenCaptureMode`, Linux and Windows always record a wireframe, and browser SDKs ignore it. Recording trigger steps of type `click`, `hover`, `navigation` and `log` match widgets, routes and log lines there; see "Recording trigger steps" below. The Flutter SDK can also send its ordinary logs, spans and metrics to another OpenTelemetry backend (`telemetry`); exceptions, messages, session and control records, OpAMP and recordings stay on Traceway. A Flutter app without a connection string runs standalone and never polls.

**Replay images** (`replay.images`: `off`, `wifi`, `always`; the SDK default is `wifi`) is offered in the rule editor of Flutter, iOS and Android projects. On Android and iOS it decides whether a wireframe replay carries pictures of image views (bitmaps downscaled and JPEG-encoded, never a screenshot of the window; `wifi` means an unmetered connection when the frame is captured; at most 4 MiB per session, then placeholders; masked images and Jetpack Compose images stay placeholders). On Flutter it keeps (`wifi`, `always`) or drops (`off`) the URL references to network images, and nothing is uploaded. The app's `replayImages` option is a ceiling: the lower of the two applies. Session events report the policy as `traceway.replay.images` and the bytes sent as `traceway.replay.image_bytes`.

**Android projects** use the same document and the same app signals: `errors`, `messages`, `console` (`System.out` lines at info, `System.err` lines at error, and `Traceway.log` at its level), `network` (OkHttp calls through `TracewayOkHttpInterceptor`, and `startRequest` / `endRequest`), `navigation` (activities and AndroidX fragments as `/ClassName`, or `Traceway.recordNavigation`), `userActions` (taps, with a view selector), `custom` and replay, which is always a wireframe of the app's windows (views and Jetpack Compose semantics, replayed as HTML; `replay.captureMode` is ignored). `replay.maskAllInputs` (on by default) masks typed text; password fields are always masked. Recording trigger steps match views, Compose nodes, screens and log lines; see "Recording trigger steps" below. Like Flutter, the Android SDK can send its ordinary logs, spans and metrics to another OpenTelemetry backend (`telemetry`), and an app without a connection string, or with `remoteConfig = false`, never polls.

**iOS projects** use the same document and the same app signals: `errors` (crashes, uncaught `NSException`s, `Traceway.captureException`), `messages` (`Traceway.captureMessage`), `console` (`Traceway.log` at its level; `print` and `NSLog` are not captured), `network` (URLSession requests as client spans from the OpenTelemetry URLSession instrumentation), `navigation` (view controllers as `/ClassName`, SwiftUI `.tracewayScreen`, or `Traceway.recordNavigation`), `userActions` (taps, with a view selector), `custom` and replay, which is always a wireframe of the view hierarchy (`replay.captureMode` is ignored). `replay.maskAllInputs` (on by default) masks typed text; secure fields are always masked. SwiftUI text is shown as its words only while an assistive technology runs on the device, otherwise as text-shaped bars. Its `app.*` performance metrics are tuned by the rule's `metrics` section like Android's and Flutter's. Like Flutter, it can send its ordinary logs and spans to another OpenTelemetry backend (`telemetry`), and an app without a connection string, or with `remoteConfig: false`, never polls.

**Page performance as metrics.** The SDK aggregates metrics on the device, independently of detailed signal modes. Keep `metrics.enabled: true` and `metrics.sampleRate: 1` for population coverage; lowering event/replay collection does not require lowering metrics. `metrics.flushSeconds` defaults to 300 (30..3600); page-hide and session-end also flush. `captureMetrics: false` is an app ceiling. A browser `2.0.0-beta.N` prerelease instead derives metrics only from uploaded performance events and streams `webVitals`; the Flutter and Android 2.x prereleases aggregate on the device and apply these settings. Read [rum.md](rum.md) for metric names, dimensions, sampling, dashboards, releases and SLOs. New browser projects receive Web Performance immediately; an empty chart is not evidence of healthy traffic.

Session start and end events are sent unless `sessions.enabled` is false. The built-in `default-exception` trigger uploads up to 10 minutes of buffered breadcrumbs and a 30-second replay clip on each exception (5-second cooldown, at most 20 per session). `recordAllSessions: true` in `init()` streams breadcrumbs and replay instead of buffering them.

## How a client's settings are decided

1. **SDK defaults**, as above.
2. **Rules**: every enabled rule whose conditions match the client adds the fields it sets, in list order, and a later rule wins. A rule holds only what it changes. Conditions test what the browser reports (`service.version`, `deployment.environment.name`, `browser.name`, `browser.version`, `os.name`, `user.id`, `session.id`, `service.instance.id`, anything the app sets with `setAttribute`), all must hold, and an optional rollout keeps the rule to a sticky percentage of clients. A rule's settings can also carry triggers and the kill switch (`enabled: false`, which turns everything off for the matching clients).
3. **Ceilings**: the `capture*`, `sessionRecording` and `sessions` options of `init()`, and what the organization's plan does not include, can never be turned back on remotely.
4. **Timed overrides**: a trigger's `stream` action, and captures, which also bring back signals a rule switched off.

**Triggers** run on the device: one to five steps matched in order (event name, signal, severity, log body with `contains`, `icontains`, `starts_with` or `glob`, span status and duration, any attribute), optionally a count within a sliding window, then actions: `flush` (upload the last N seconds, optionally with a replay clip), `stream`, `startReplay`, `emit` (a marker event) or `capture`. There is no regular expression operator on purpose.

### Recording trigger steps

The rule editor's **Recording triggers** builder writes steps that name a user journey: `{"match":{"event":{"type":"click","value":"#pay"}}}`, with `type` one of `click`, `hover`, `navigation` or `log` and an optional `withinSeconds` after the previous step. The same step means different things on the two platforms, because a Flutter app has no DOM and no URL.

| Step | Browser | Flutter (the builder says **Tap** and **Widget selector**) |
|---|---|---|
| `click` | The clicked element or an ancestor matches the CSS selector | The widget under the finger or a widget above it matches the selector |
| `hover` | A pointer enters a matching element, never touch | A mouse pointer enters a matching widget, desktop only |
| `navigation` | The pathname of the page's URL; `/users/{id}` matches one segment | The path of the route arrived at: its name, else `/` and the page widget's type (`/CheckoutPage`), else `/` and the route's type |
| `log` | A console line, an OpenTelemetry log record or `captureMessage`, with a level | A `print` / `debugPrint` line or `captureMessage`; every line is at info, so the builder offers no level |

In a Flutter project the selector syntax reads widgets: `ElevatedButton` is the widget type, `#pay` is `Key('pay')` or `Semantics(identifier: 'pay')`, `.button` is a `Semantics` role, and the only attributes are `[key=...]`, `[identifier=...]`, `[label=...]` (semantics label or tooltip), `[text=...]` (the text shown) and `[type=...]`. There are no element ids, classes or `data-*` attributes. Keys and semantics identifiers are the stable names; text changes with the wording and the language, and type names are minified in `--obfuscate` builds.

Nobody has to work a Flutter selector out. Every tap is recorded with a selector the SDK checked against the tapped widget (`ElevatedButton#pay`, or `ElevatedButton[text="Print Log Lines"]` when the button has no key), shown in the **Actions** list of a session and stored as the `browser.css_selector` attribute of the `browser.user_action.click` log record. Navigation rows of the same list show the route paths a navigation step is compared with. Navigation is reported only where the app attached `Traceway.navigatorObserver` or calls `Traceway.recordNavigation(path)`.

A push or a replace arrives at the new route and a pop arrives at the route it returns to, so a step for `/` also matches coming back to the home screen. Full rules: https://docs.tracewayapp.com/client/flutter#recording-triggers

In an Android project the builder also says **Tap** and **View selector**, and the selector reads views and Jetpack Compose semantics nodes: `MaterialButton` is the view class or any superclass (`Button` matches a `MaterialButton`; a Compose node's type is its role, `Button`, `Checkbox`, `Switch`, `Tab`, `Image`, or its kind, `Text`, `TextField`, `Slider`), `#pay` is `android:id="@+id/pay"` (the resource entry name) or `Modifier.testTag("pay")`, `.button` is a role (`button`, `link`, `header`, `image`, `textField`, `slider`, `checkbox`, `toggle`, `selected`), and the attributes are `[key=...]` (`android:tag`), `[identifier=...]`, `[label=...]` (content description or tooltip), `[text=...]` (the text shown, never an input's content) and `[type=...]`. A tap matches the view under the finger or any of its parents; hover needs a mouse. Navigation steps match the screen on top: `/` and the activity's or fragment's class (`/CheckoutActivity`, `/CartFragment`), or the path the app passes to `Traceway.recordNavigation("/orders/{id}")` from Compose Navigation or another router. Ids, test tags, roles, labels and text survive R8; class names may be renamed in a minified build (a renamed class is named by its nearest superclass that kept its name). Every tap is a `browser.user_action.click` record with the selector the SDK checked in `browser.css_selector` (`MaterialButton#pay`), shown in a session's **Actions** list. Full rules: https://docs.tracewayapp.com/client/android#recording-triggers

In an iOS project the builder says **Tap** and **View selector** and offers no hover step (a hover never matches on iOS). The selector reads UIKit views: `UIButton` is the view's class (without module or generic arguments, any case), `#pay` is `accessibilityIdentifier = "pay"`, `.button` is a role from the view's accessibility traits or class (`button`, `link`, `header`, `image`, `textField`, `slider`, `toggle`, `selected`), and the attributes are `[key=...]` (the view's `tag`), `[identifier=...]`, `[label=...]` (`accessibilityLabel`), `[text=...]` (a label's text or a button's title, never what is typed into a field) and `[type=...]`. A tap matches the view under the finger or any superview. SwiftUI controls have no views of their own, so a SwiftUI tap names the hosting view; target SwiftUI screens with navigation steps. Navigation steps match `/` and the class of the view controller that appeared (`/CheckoutViewController`, or `/ContentView` for a hosting controller), or the path the app reports with `.tracewayScreen("/checkout")` or `Traceway.recordNavigation("/orders/{id}")`. Every tap is a `browser.user_action.click` record with the selector the SDK checked in `browser.css_selector` (`UIButton#pay`). Full rules: https://docs.tracewayapp.com/client/ios#recording-triggers

**Captures** make one target upload what it was holding (the lookback, 10 minutes by default) and stream everything for 1 minute to 24 hours. A target is a device (`service.instance.id`), a user (`user.id`), a session or any attribute and value. At most 20 are active per project, and a client under a capture polls every 60 seconds. Start one from **New Capture**, from **Capture this device** on a session page, or from **Capture device** (or user, or session) on an issue's event card. A trigger's `capture` action starts one on the device itself. Capture status reads **Waiting for client**, **Delivered · awaiting acknowledgement**, **Applied · awaiting data**, **Collecting**, **Expired · no data received**, **Completed** or **Cancelled**, and reflects at least one matching browser, not every one.

**Preview** shows the document a client with given attributes (and optionally an instance id, which decides rollout buckets) receives from the saved rules and active captures, with plan limits applied. It does not know the app's `init()` options or whether a browser has polled, so it is not proof of what a live browser runs.

## Seeing it work

The SDK reports what it did as log records of the browser, Flutter, iOS or Android project that always stream unless the kill switch is on: `traceway.config.applied` (with the config hash), `traceway.trigger.fired` and `traceway.capture.started`. Breadcrumbs that were sent are stored once, as log records and spans tagged with `session.id`. The session page reads them for the whole session, and an issue's event card reads the 10 minutes before the exception. A session's overview shows the version of the SDK that recorded it (**JavaScript SDK**, **Flutter SDK** or **Android SDK**), which tells a 2.x client from a 1.x one.

## Reading and changing it from an agent

| Task | CLI | MCP tool |
|---|---|---|
| List the rules in order, with `updatedAt` | `traceway opamp rules list` | `list_sdk_config_rules` |
| Preview what a client gets | `traceway opamp preview --file client.json` with `{"attributes":{...},"instanceUid":"..."}` | `preview_sdk_config` |
| Create a rule (write) | `traceway-write opamp rules create --file rule.json` | `create_sdk_config_rule` |
| Replace a rule (write) | `traceway-write opamp rules update <id> --file rule.json --expected-updated-at <updatedAt>` | `update_sdk_config_rule` |
| Reorder or delete rules (write) | `traceway-write opamp rules reorder <id>...` / `delete <id>` | `reorder_sdk_config_rules` / `delete_sdk_config_rule` |

Rule writes follow the three opt-in levels in `organization.md`, and the `traceway-write` skill has the playbook. A rule can stream breadcrumbs for every visitor, turn on full-session replay or set `replay.maskAllInputs: false`, so say what a change collects before saving it. Captures are dashboard only, for reading and starting alike.
